rationale: The hypothesis posits that increased body weight or obesity is a recurrent finding in FBXO11-related intellectual developmental disorder that occurs in over 50% of specific cohorts, distinguishing it from syndromic ID entities characterized by growth failure. Literature evidence confirms that increased body weight reached 58.3% (7/12) in a cohort of 12 individuals from 5 Chinese families (Pan et al., 2024). However, in larger international de novo cohorts, obesity or increased weight is only present in a minority of patients: 25% (5/20) in Gregor et al. (2018) and ~17.4% (4/23) in Gregor et al. (2022). Furthermore, short stature is also frequently present in FBXO11 patients (6/12 in Pan et al., 2024; 4/20 in Gregor et al., 2018), showing bidirectional somatic growth dysregulation rather than a uniform distinguishing metabolic phenotype against growth-deficient syndromes.

evidence.text: In a study of 12 individuals with intellectual disability from 5 Chinese families harboring FBXO11 variants, increased body weight was observed in 7 of 12 patients, while short stature was also observed in 6 of 12 patients.

source.title: FBXO11 variants are associated with intellectual disability and variable clinical manifestation in Chinese affected individuals
source.quote: Almost all the affected individuals presented with mild to severe intellectual disability (12/12), global developmental delay (10/12), speech and language development delay (8/12) associated with a range of alternate features including increased body weight (7/12), short stature (6/12), seizures (3/12)

evidence.text: In the initial cohort defining FBXO11 neurodevelopmental disorder in 20 individuals, obesity was identified in only 5 of 20 individuals (25%), alongside short stature in 4 of 20 and tall stature in 2 of 20.

source.title: De novo variants in the F-box protein FBXO11 in 20 individuals with a variable neurodevelopmental disorder
source.journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics
source.quote: They present with mild to severe developmental delay associated with a range of features including short (4/20) or tall (2/20) stature, obesity (5/20), microcephaly (4/19) or macrocephaly (2/19), behavioral problems (17/20), seizures (5/20)

evidence.text: In an expanded study assessing 23 additional individuals with de novo FBXO11 variants, increased body weight and/or hyperphagia were documented in only 4 individuals, noting an enrichment primarily in individuals harboring likely gene disrupting (LGD) variants.

source.title: De novo missense variants in FBXO11 alter its protein expression and subcellular localization
source.quote: Increased body weight and/or hyperphagia were reported in four individuals. Overweight/hyperphagia were more common in individuals carrying LGD variants

numbers.metric: increased body weight or hyperphagia frequency

conflicts: Increased body weight exceeded 50% in one familial Chinese cohort (7/12, 58.3%), but occurred in only 25% (5/20) and 17.4% (4/23) in larger multicenter cohorts of de novo FBXO11 variants.

Short stature and impaired somatic growth occur in 50% (6/12) of the Chinese cohort and 20% (4/20) of the initial Gregor cohort, contradicting the notion that the syndrome is uniformly distinguishable from growth-failure entities.

new_directions.question_text: Does FBXO11 variant type (loss-of-function/truncating vs missense) systematically govern metabolic phenotype vs growth failure?
new_directions.rationale: Gregor et al. (2022) observed that overweight/hyperphagia was enriched in likely gene disrupting (LGD) variants compared to missense variants, which could explain differing frequencies across cohorts.

new_directions.question_text: Is increased body weight in FBXO11-related disorder age-dependent, emerging primarily in older children and adolescents rather than infants?
new_directions.rationale: Neurodevelopmental obesity syndromes often present with early hypotonia and feeding difficulties in infancy followed by hyperphagia and weight gain in later childhood.
